title: Advanced Features: EWMA, Quality Control, and Cohort Analysis
text: Traditional ACWR uses rolling averages (RA). EWMA method, introduced Williams et al. (2017), offers: - Greater sensitivity recent training changes - Customizable decay rates via half-life parameters - Confidence bands via bootstrap quantify uncertainty Reference: Williams, S., et al. (2017). Better way determine acute:chronic workload ratio? British Journal Sports Medicine, 51(3), 209-210. DOI: 10.1136/bjsports-2016-096589

title: Advanced Features: EWMA, Quality Control, and Cohort Analysis
text: Key differences: - RA: Equal weight days window; sudden jumps old workouts exit window - EWMA: Exponential decay; smooth transitions; responsive recent changes
code: # Load activities activities <- load_local_activities("export_12345678.zip")  # Calculate ACWR using Rolling Average (traditional) acwr_ra <- calculate_acwr_ewma(   activities,   activity_type = "Run",   method = "ra",   acute_period = 7,   chronic_period = 28,   load_metric = "duration_mins" )  # Calculate ACWR using EWMA acwr_ewma <- calculate_acwr_ewma(   activities,   activity_type = "Run",   method = "ewma",   half_life_acute = 3.5, # Acute load half-life (days)   half_life_chronic = 14, # Chronic load half-life (days)   load_metric = "duration_mins" )  # Compare the two methods library(ggplot2) ggplot() +   geom_line(     data = acwr_ra, aes(x = date, y = acwr_smooth),     color = "blue", linewidth = 1, linetype = "solid"   ) +   geom_line(     data = acwr_ewma, aes(x = date, y = acwr_smooth),     color = "red", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed"   ) +   labs(     title = "ACWR: Rolling Average vs EWMA",     subtitle = "Blue = RA (7:28d) | Red = EWMA (3.5:14d half-life)",     x = "Date", y = "ACWR"   ) +   theme_minimal()

title: Advanced Features: EWMA, Quality Control, and Cohort Analysis
text: Confidence bands quantify uncertainty ACWR estimates, essential research reporting. Interpretation: - Gray band: 95% confidence interval moving-block bootstrap - Wider bands = uncertainty (e.g., high load variability) - Narrower bands = stable estimates
code: # Calculate EWMA with 95% confidence bands acwr_ewma_ci <- calculate_acwr_ewma(   activities,   activity_type = "Run",   method = "ewma",   half_life_acute = 3.5,   half_life_chronic = 14,   load_metric = "duration_mins",   ci = TRUE, # Enable confidence intervals   B = 200, # Bootstrap iterations   block_len = 7, # Block length (days) for bootstrap   conf_level = 0.95 # 95% CI )  # Plot with confidence bands ggplot(acwr_ewma_ci, aes(x = date)) +   geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = acwr_lower, ymax = acwr_upper),     fill = "gray70", alpha = 0.5   ) +   geom_line(aes(y = acwr_smooth), color = "black", linewidth = 1) +   geom_hline(yintercept = c(0.8, 1.3), linetype = "dotted", color = "green") +   geom_hline(yintercept = 1.5, linetype = "dotted", color = "red") +   labs(     title = "ACWR with 95% Confidence Bands",     subtitle = "Gray band = bootstrap confidence interval",     x = "Date", y = "ACWR"   ) +   theme_minimal()

text: ’s complete research workflow combining features:
code: library(Athlytics) library(dplyr) library(ggplot2)  # --- Step 1: Load multi-athlete cohort --- cohort_files <- c("athlete1_export.zip", "athlete2_export.zip", "athlete3_export.zip") cohort_data <- lapply(cohort_files, function(file) {   load_local_activities(file) |>     mutate(athlete_id = tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(file))) }) |> bind_rows()  # --- Step 2: Quality control (conceptual - for stream data) --- # If you have stream data, flag quality before calculating metrics # stream <- parse_activity_file("path/to/activity.fit") # flagged <- flag_quality(stream, sport = "Run") # summary <- summarize_quality(flagged)  # --- Step 3: Calculate ACWR with EWMA + CI --- cohort_acwr <- cohort_data |>   group_by(athlete_id) |>   group_modify(~ calculate_acwr_ewma(     .x,     activity_type = "Run",     method = "ewma",     half_life_acute = 3.5,     half_life_chronic = 14,     load_metric = "duration_mins",     ci = TRUE,     B = 100 # Reduced for speed in example   )) |>   ungroup() |>   mutate(type = "Run")  # --- Step 4: Calculate cohort reference --- reference <- calculate_cohort_reference(   cohort_acwr,   metric = "acwr_smooth",   by = c("type"),   probs = c(0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95),   min_athletes = 3 )  # --- Step 5: Visualize individual with confidence + cohort --- individual <- cohort_acwr |> filter(athlete_id == "athlete1")  p <- plot_with_reference(individual, reference, metric = "acwr_smooth") +   # Add individual's confidence bands   geom_ribbon(     data = individual,     aes(x = date, ymin = acwr_lower, ymax = acwr_upper),     fill = "blue", alpha = 0.2   )  print(p)  # --- Step 6: Export for statistical analysis --- write.csv(cohort_acwr, "cohort_acwr_with_ci.csv", row.names = FALSE) write.csv(reference, "cohort_reference.csv", row.names = FALSE)

Correct interpretation: - “Athlete 75th percentile cohort” ✅ - “Athlete’s ACWR significantly higher cohort” ❌ (requires statistical test) Minimum sample sizes: - P25-P75: n ≥ 5 athletes - P5-P95: n ≥ 20 athletes (stable extremes)

title: Advanced Features: EWMA, Quality Control, and Cohort Analysis
text: Q: choose EWMA half-life? : Start defaults (3.5:14d ≈ 7:28d RA). responsive monitoring, reduce proportionally (e.g., 2.5:10d). smoother trends, increase (e.g., 5:20d). Q: Bootstrap slow. Can reduce B? : Yes. B = 50–100 often sufficient visual inspection. publication, use B = 200–500. Q: cohort < 5 athletes? : Set min_athletes = 3, report limitation. Percentiles n < 5 unstable. Q: Can use methods injury prediction? : . descriptive monitoring tools. Injury prediction requires proper case-control studies, controlling confounders, validation. See: Carey, D. L., et al. (2018). Predictive modelling training loads injury Australian football. International Journal Computer Science Sport, 17(1), 49-66. DOI: 10.2478/ijcss-2018-0002; Impellizzeri, F. M., et al. (2021). role chronic workloads play acute chronic workload ratio? Time dismiss ACWR underlying theory. Sports Medicine, 51(3), 581-592. DOI: 10.1007/s40279-020-01378-6 Q: cite Athlytics? : Use standard software citation format version number repository URL. See main tutorial complete citation.

title: Getting Started with Athlytics
text: EF? Efficiency Factor measures much output (speed/power) generate per unit input (heart rate). ’s key indicator aerobic fitness improvements. Metrics: speed_hr (running) — Speed (m/s) / HR: Higher values = faster HR = better aerobic fitness gap_hr (running hilly terrain) — Grade Adjusted Speed (m/s) / HR: Accounts elevation changes using Strava’s GAP data. Recommended hilly routes raw speed doesn’t reflect true effort. power_hr (cycling) — Power (W) / HR: Higher values = power HR = better aerobic fitness Handling Elevation: hilly runs, use ef_metric = "gap_hr" account gradient. uses Strava’s Grade Adjusted Pace (GAP) data, represents equivalent flat-ground speed (m/s) adjusted terrain gradient, providing accurate efficiency comparisons across varied terrain. Changes Mean: Increasing EF = Aerobic fitness improving (work HR) Stable EF = Maintaining current fitness Decreasing EF = Fatigue, overtraining, fitness loss

text: Best Practices: Track trends weeks/months, day--day fluctuations Use steady-state efforts — Interval workouts skew results. package uses coefficient variation (CV) thresholds identify steady-state segments, common approach exercise physiology (Coyle & González-Alonso, 2001). Consider external factors — Heat, altitude, fatigue affect EF Scientific Background: Steady-state exercise characterized relatively constant oxygen consumption heart rate (CV < 8-10%). package automatically filters non-steady activities ensure EF calculations reflect true aerobic efficiency rather pacing artifacts. See: Coyle, E. F., & González-Alonso, J. (2001). Cardiovascular drift prolonged exercise. Exercise Sport Sciences Reviews, 29(2), 88-92. DOI: 10.1097/00003677-200104000-00009; Allen, H., Coggan, . R., & McGregor, S. (2019). Training Racing Power Meter (3rd ed.). VeloPress. ISBN: 978-1-937715-93-9 Time-based rolling window: Window size derived stream’s median sampling interval, targeting 300-second centered window respecting minimum maximum row caps. Coefficient Variation (CV): window position, CV = rolling SD / rolling mean calculated primary metric (velocity running, power cycling). Contiguous steady-state blocks: Data points CV < steady_cv_threshold (default 8%) grouped continuous steady-state blocks rather pooled across scattered intervals. Minimum duration: EF decoupling require contiguous steady-state block spanning least min_steady_minutes (default 20 minutes EF, 40 minutes decoupling). Aggregation: EF decoupling computed accepted steady-state block, using median-based aggregation reduce sensitivity outliers. Practical Analysis:
code:
# Calculate monthly average EF library(lubridate)  ef_monthly <- ef_runs |>   mutate(month = floor_date(date, "month")) |>   group_by(month) |>   summarise(     mean_ef = mean(ef_value, na.rm = TRUE),     n_activities = n()   ) |>   arrange(desc(month))  print(ef_monthly)  # Compare first vs last 3 months recent_ef <- ef_runs |>   filter(date >= Sys.Date() - 90) |>   pull(ef_value) baseline_ef <- ef_runs |>   filter(date < Sys.Date() - 90, date >= Sys.Date() - 180) |>   pull(ef_value)  cat(sprintf(   "Recent EF: %.2f
Baseline EF: %.2f
Change: %.1f%%
",   mean(recent_ef, na.rm = TRUE),   mean(baseline_ef, na.rm = TRUE),   (mean(recent_ef, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(baseline_ef, na.rm = TRUE) - 1) * 100 ))

title: Getting Started with Athlytics
text: EF tracks aerobic efficiency across activities time, decoupling looks within single activity measure efficiency changes start finish. Decoupling? Decoupling quantifies cardiovascular drift—phenomenon heart rate gradually rises prolonged efforts even speed/power remains constant. Low decoupling indicates good aerobic endurance. Works: function compares efficiency (speed/HR power/HR) first half second half activity: Decoupling %=EFfirst half−EFsecond halfEFfirst half×100 \text{Decoupling \%} = \frac{\text{EF}_{\text{first half}} - \text{EF}_{\text{second half}}}{\text{EF}_{\text{first half}}} \times 100 Positive values = efficiency decline second half (HR drift); <5% commonly used reference threshold, requires interpretation context steady-state environmental conditions (Coyle & González-Alonso, 2001; Friel, 2009). Interpretation: < 5% — Excellent aerobic base, well-adapted 5-10% — Acceptable, drift manageable > 10% — Significant drift (fatigue, heat, insufficient base fitness)

", nrow(runs)))  # ---- 2. Training Load Monitoring ---- acwr_data <- calculate_acwr(   activities_data = runs,   activity_type = "Run",   load_metric = "duration_mins" )  # Check current training status current_acwr <- acwr_data |>   filter(date >= Sys.Date() - 30) |>   tail(1) |>   pull(acwr_smooth)  cat(sprintf("Current ACWR: %.2f
", current_acwr))  # Visualize p1 <- plot_acwr(acwr_data, highlight_zones = TRUE) +   labs(title = "6-Month Training Load Progression") print(p1)  # ---- 3. Aerobic Fitness Tracking ---- ef_data <- calculate_ef(   activities_data = runs,   activity_type = "Run",   ef_metric = "speed_hr",   export_dir = export_path )  # Calculate fitness trend ef_trend <- ef_data |>   mutate(month = lubridate::floor_date(date, "month")) |>   group_by(month) |>   summarise(mean_ef = mean(ef_value, na.rm = TRUE))  p2 <- plot_ef(ef_data, add_trend_line = TRUE) +   labs(title = "Aerobic Efficiency Trend") print(p2)  # ---- 4. ",   avg_decouple,   ifelse(avg_decouple < 5, "excellent",     ifelse(avg_decouple < 10, "good", "needs work")   ) ))  p3 <- plot_decoupling(data = decoupling_data) +   labs(title = "Cardiovascular Drift in Long Runs") print(p3)  # ---- 5. title: Calculate Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio (ACWR) — calculate_acwr
text: Computes Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio (ACWR) local Strava activity data using rolling average methods. ACWR key metric monitoring training load balance athletes (Gabbett, 2016; Hulin et al., 2016). Algorithm: Daily Aggregation: Sum activities date compute daily load Complete Time Series: Fill missing days zero load (critical ACWR accuracy) Acute Load (ATL): Rolling mean acute_period days (default: 7) Chronic Load (CTL): Rolling mean chronic_period days (default: 28) ACWR Calculation: ATL / CTL (set NA CTL < 0.01 avoid division zero) Smoothing: Optional rolling mean smoothing_period days visualization Data Requirements: function automatically fetches additional historical data (chronic_period days start_date) ensure accurate chronic load calculations analysis start point. Ensure Strava export contains sufficient historical activities. Load Metric Implementations: "tss": Uses normalized power (NP) FTP approximate Training Stress Score (TSS). Formula: (duration_sec × NP × ) / (FTP × 3600) × 100, = NP/FTP (equivalently: hours × ^2 × 100). "hrss": HR-based load using heart rate reserve (simplified TRIMP; TrainingPeaks hrTSS). Formula: duration_sec * (HR - resting_HR) / (max_HR - resting_HR). Descriptive ACWR Bands: ACWR < 0.8: Recent load chronic load ACWR 0.8-1.3: Commonly used training-load reference band ACWR 1.3-1.5: Elevated recent/chronic load ratio ACWR > 1.5: High ACWR ratio / load-spike band Multi-Athlete Studies: cohort analyses, add athlete_id column calculation use group_by(athlete_id) group_modify(). See examples vignettes details.

title: Calculate ACWR using EWMA Method with Confidence Bands — calculate_acwr_ewma
text: function extends basic ACWR calculation two methods: RA (Rolling Average): Traditional rolling mean approach (default). EWMA (Exponentially Weighted Moving Average): Uses exponential decay configurable half-lives. responsive recent changes. EWMA Formula: smoothing parameter alpha calculated half-life: alpha = 1 - exp(-ln(2) / half_life). EWMA update : E_t = alpha * L_t + (1-alpha) * E_{t-1} L_t daily load E_t exponentially weighted average. Confidence Bands: ci = TRUE method = "ewma", uses moving-block bootstrap estimate uncertainty. daily load sequence resampled overlapping weekly blocks (preserving within-week correlation), ACWR recalculated, percentiles form confidence bands. accounts temporal correlation training load patterns.

text: Calculates aerobic decoupling (HR drift relative speed/power) using detailed activity stream data local FIT/TCX/GPX files. Provides data plot_decoupling. Compares output/HR efficiency first second halves activities. Positive values indicate HR drift (cardiovascular drift). Best practice: Use load_local_activities() load data, pass function. function parses FIT/TCX/GPX files Strava export extract detailed stream data (time, heartrate, distance/power). Activities split two halves, efficiency factor (output/HR) compared halves. Steady-State Detection Method: computing decoupling, function applies rolling coefficient variation (CV) filter identify steady-state segments: sliding window (default 300 s) computes rolling mean standard deviation output metric (velocity power). CV (= rolling SD / rolling mean) calculated time point. Time points CV < steady_cv_threshold (default 8 %) classified steady-state. least min_steady_minutes contiguous steady-state data must present; otherwise activity marked "insufficient_steady_duration". Rolling window: sliding window targeting 300 seconds (capped nrow / 4, floor 60 seconds' worth samples) computes rolling mean SD output metric. CV calculation: CV = rolling SD / rolling mean time point. title: Athlytics 1.0.5
text: calculate_ef() stream path now uses continuous-block steady-state detection. Previously EF computed median ratio across every scattered point whose rolling CV cleared steady_cv_threshold, interval workout three short “steady islands” silently pass min_steady_minutes gate. stream path now mirrors calculate_decoupling(): uses rle() find contiguous steady runs accepts activities whose longest run lasts least min_steady_minutes. New output columns steady_duration_minutes, n_steady_blocks, sampling_interval_seconds make accepted block auditable; new status code "insufficient_steady_duration" distinguishes old "non_steady". gap_hr stream-path fallback now explicit. stream grade-adjusted channel function still falls back plain speed/HR, returned row now records via ef_metric_requested = "gap_hr", ef_metric_used = "speed_hr", new status string "gap_stream_unavailable_fallback_to_speed". Downstream consumers need strict GAP semantics can now filter columns instead assuming ef_metric argument equals metric actually computed. Rolling windows now time-based, row-based. calculate_ef(), calculate_decoupling(), flag_quality() previously assumed 1 Hz sampling (window_size <- 300 rows). effective window silently rescaled 0.5 Hz smart-recording multi-Hz streams. new internal estimate_sampling_interval() helper reads diff(time) three functions now target wall-clock windows; observed interval exposed sampling_interval_seconds EF/decoupling output attr(result, "sampling_interval_seconds") flag_quality output. flag_quality() HR / power jump thresholds honour “per-second” documentation. max_hr_jump = 10 now compared |dHR/dt| (bpm / s) rather raw sample--sample differences; change applies max_pw_jump. Streams exactly 1 Hz therefore judged consistently across recording devices. Training-load calculation now distinguishes rest days missing-data training days. compute_single_load() returns list(value, status) instead collapsing every non-computable case 0. calculate_acwr(), calculate_acwr_ewma(), calculate_exposure() gain missing_load = c("zero", "na") argument: "zero" (default) preserves historical behaviour, "na" keeps NA days whose load computed rolling means visibly propagate gap.
